newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic weakness rules out civil war-opposition.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic weakness rules out civil war-opposition.

text.p: A leader of the pro-democracy movement in Serbia on Friday dismissed fears of a civil war, saying President Slobodan Milosevic's authority had declined so much there was little danger of major violence.

Zoran Djindjic, a leader of the Zajedno (Together) bloc that has mounted 46 consecutive days of street rallies against vote fraud, said demonstrators would soldier on until the ruling Socialists (SPS) reinstated the election outcome.

He expected no SPS concessions before early summer, but ruled out any degeneration of peaceful protests into civil conflict despite a 10-day-old ban on street marches that has heightened the risk of confrontations with police.

"The basis of Milosevic's authority has been diminished to such an extent that he cannot provoke a civil war because there are not enough people who would want, or have an interest to, wage war for him," Djindjic said.

"The only conceivable form of violence is conflict between demonstrators and police, but it cannot be of large proportion. The danger is not as major as (previously) supposed," he told Reuters Television in an interview.

Dissension over Milosevic's annulment of local elections won by the opposition has emerged in the army, the Serbian Orthodox Church and even the security police, all mainstays of autocratic leftist government in federal Yugoslavia up to now.

Djindjic is the leader of the Democratic Party and has been thrust into prominence by the opposition protests. He was speaking before publication in Vienna of a letter from the Yugoslav government which appeared to accept at least in part the opposition case.

The letter from Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic to the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said the Zajedno coalition had won a majority in nine municipalities in Belgrade.
The letter was a response to a report on the disputed municipal elections drawn up last week by former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez after a fact-finding mission.
Gonzalez concluded that Zajedno had fairly won November 17 elections in 15 of Serbia's 18 biggest cities and urged Milosevic to honour the results.
The reclusive Serbian strongman has remained silent on Gonzalez's report and the SPS-dominated mainstream media have ignored or denounced Zajedno demonstrators as alleged stooges of a bullying West.

Western governments have warned Milosevic to democratise Serbia or be denied financial aid for the economy, teetering on the brink of collapse from SPS corruption and 54 months of U.N. sanctions imposed for stoking the 43-month war Bosnia.

In his televised New Year's message, Milosevic promised significant free-market reforms in 1997, but made no mention of domestic or foreign pressures to end monolithic rule prevailing in Yugoslavia since 1945.

Analysts said debate was raging in Milosevic's circle between moderates prepared to risk slackening the SPS grip on power to open the Western financial pipeline and hardliners ready to hunker down behind a siege economy.

Thousands of Zajedno supporters beat pots and pans in their flats on Thursday after Belgrade students urged citizens to make a daily hullabaloo drowning out -- at least symbolically -- state television's main newscast.
The ear-splitting din was heard in most Belgrade districts aside from Dedinje where Milosevic and other members of the ruling elite live in well-guarded homes.

Street marches through the capital were banned on December 24 when Milosevic bused about 40,000 loyalists from the provinces into Belgrade to intimidate Zajedno. A riot ensued, killing one person and injuring more than 50.
About 250,000 Zajedno faithful welcomed the New Year in Belgrade with a city-centre rally featuring ringing alarm clocks in a shrill warning to Milosevic that his "time is up".

In a separate interview with German radio, Djindjic said solidarity with Zajedno voiced from the church and elements of the army would strengthen its position but would not make a big difference in the short term.
